title: Adaptive Surrogate Gradients for Sequential Reinforcement Learning in Spik

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states $\tilde{\sigma}'_k(z) = \sigma'(kz)/k = \sigma(kz)\cdot(1-\sigma(kz))$. This is mathematically incorrect: since $\sigma'(kz)=\sigma(kz)(1-\sigma(kz))$ by the chain rule, dividing by $k$ gives $\sigma(kz)(1-\sigma(kz))/k$, not $\sigma(kz)(1-\sigma(kz))$. The stated equality only holds when $k=1$, yet it is presented as a general identity used throughout the subsequent derivation.

The appendix claims the surrogate gradient generally satisfies $\tilde\sigma'_k(z) > \sigma'(z)$ for most z 'unless k=1', implying steeper slopes (larger k) produce a larger (positively biased) gradient magnitude than the true gradient. This directly contradicts the main text and Figure 1b, which show that steeper slopes (k=100) cause vanishing gradients in deep layers while shallower slopes (k=1) increase gradient magnitude — i.e., the bias direction is reversed relative to what is claimed here.

Section 3.4 states the critic 'receives all observed states without any action history, maintaining architectural symmetry with the deployed actor,' directly contradicting Section 3.1, which states 'Both the guiding policy and the non-spiking critic receive privileged information in the form of action histories.' This also contradicts the section title 'Asymmetric Actor-Critic', which by definition requires the critic to use privileged/asymmetric information not available to the actor.

The table caption states 'The ANN without action history did not manage to stabilize the quadrotor,' and the main text reiterates 'ANNs without action history failed to control the drone.' Yet Table 3 reports a specific Position Error of 0.25 m for this model, implying measurable, meaningful flight data was collected — inconsistent with a complete failure to stabilize (while Trajectory Error is marked N/A for the same model, consistent with failure).

Reference [15] is 'Crazyflie 2.0 quadrotor as a platform for research and education in robotics and control engineering,' but the text cites it in support of describing the 'Crazyflie 2.1 platform,' a version mismatch between the cited source and the claimed hardware.

The discussion abruptly references comparing methods 'on the Teensy,' a hardware platform never introduced elsewhere in the paper (the deployment platform throughout is described as the Crazyflie 2.1). This is inconsistent with the methodology described, suggesting either an error or an undocumented hardware platform.

TD3BC uses hidden sizes [256, 256] while BC, TD3BC+JSRL, and TD3 all use [256, 128], and TD3 uses 1M steps per epoch while all other methods use 2M steps per epoch. This undermines the claim that methods were compared 'under the same conditions' (as stated in the Abstract), since both network capacity and training budget differ across baselines.

The text states that $C_{rp}, C_{rv}, C_{rq}$ 'penalize deviations from desired states' and that 'penalty coefficients' are linearly interpolated 'from lenient to strict values over training,' implying all three curriculum-adjusted. However, Table 5 shows $C_{rq}$ constant at 0.25 (Start = End), inconsistent with the stated curriculum design for that term.

The Abstract and Conclusion report 'an average return of 400 points' for the proposed method, while Table 4 (ablation, BC-term=Yes, Jump-start=Yes, i.e. the full method) reports a reward of 412, a discrepancy not explained in the text.

The paper claims the estimated energy (9.7×10⁻⁵ mJ) is 'in line with' real-world measurements from Paredes-Valles et al. of 7×10⁻³ mJ, despite this being roughly two orders of magnitude larger, and the comparison to Wang et al. is asserted without presenting the actual comparator value, making the 'in line with' claim unsupported/misleading.
